passages.original: Prima parte libri probat perseverantiam illam, qua in Christo perseveratur usque in finem, esse doMum Dei. Hoc enim a Deo irrisorie peti, si a Deo dari non creditur. Porro dominica oratione nihil pene aliud posci quam perseverautiam juxta Cypriani martyris expositionem : qua quidem expositione ipsi gratiæ inimici convicti sunt antequam naH. Perseverandi gratiam non secundum accipientium merita, sed aliis Dei misericordia dari, aliis justo ejus judicio non dari docet.
passages.english: In the first part of the book he proves that the perseverance by which one perseveres in Christ to the end is a gift of God. For this is asked of God mockingly if it is not believed to be given by God. Further, [he proves] that in the Lord's Prayer almost nothing else is asked for than perseverance, according to the exposition of the martyr Cyprian; and by this exposition the very enemies of grace were refuted before they were born. He teaches that the grace of persevering is not given according to the merits of those who receive it, but is given to some by God's mercy, and not given to others by his just judgement.
passages.notes: This is a summary (argument) of the book, not Augustine's own text. 'doMum' read as 'donum'; 'perseverautiam' as 'perseverantiam'; 'naH' as 'nati'.

passages.original: CAPUT IV. —7. Quarta petitio est, Panem nostrum quotidianum da nobis hodie. Ubi beatus Cyprianus ostendit quomodo et hic intelligatur persevcranlia postulari. Ait quippe inter caetera : « Hunc autem panem dari nobis quotidie postulamus, ne qui iii Christo sumus, et Eucharistiam quotidie ad cibum salutis accipimus, intercedente aliquo graviore de- • licto, dum abstenti et non communicantes a cœlesti pane prohibemur, a Christi corpore separemur. » Hæc verba sancti hominis Dei, perseverantiam prorsus a Domino sanctos indicant poscere, quando hac intentione dicunt, Panem nostrum quotidianum da nobis hodie;
passages.english: CHAPTER IV. — 7. The fourth petition is, "Give us this day our daily bread." Here the blessed Cyprian shows how perseverance is understood to be asked for in this also. For he says, among other things: "We ask that this bread be given to us daily, so that we who are in Christ, and daily receive the Eucharist as the food of salvation, may not, through some graver sin intervening, while we are kept back and not communicating and are barred from the heavenly bread, be separated from the body of Christ." These words of a holy man of God show that the saints plainly ask perseverance from the Lord when they say with this intention, "Give us this day our daily bread";

passages.original: Unusquisque enim tentatur, at scriptum est, a concupiscentia sua abstractus et illectus : Deus autem neninem tentat (Jacobi i, 14, 13) ; tentatione scilicet noxia. Nam est et utilis, qua non decipimur * vel opprimi mur, sed probaMur, secundum quod dictum est, Proba me, Domine, et tenta me (Psal. xxv, 2). Illa ergo noxia tentatione, quam signilicat Apostolus, dicens, Ne forte tentaverit vos qui tentat, et inanis sit tabor noster (I Thess. III, £), Deus, ut dixi, neminem tentat, boc est, neminem infert vel inducit in tentationem. Nam tentari et in tentationem non inferri, non est matum, imo etiam bonum eat : hoc est enim probari. Quod itaque dicimus Dee, Ne noa inferasin tentationem; quid dicimus, nisi, Ne nos inferri Ii,. nas? Unde sic orant nonnulli, et legitur in codicibus pluribus, et hoc sic posuit beatissimus Cyprianus « Ne patiaris noa induci in tentationem. In Evangelio tamen graeco nusquam inveni, nisi, Ne nos inferas in tentationem. Tutiores igitur vivimus, si totum Deo damus; non amem nos illi ex parte, et nobis ex parte committtimus ; quod vidit iste venerabilis martyr.
passages.english: For each one is tempted, as it is written, when drawn away and enticed by his own desire; but God tempts no one (James 1:14, 13) — that is, with harmful temptation. For there is also a useful [temptation], by which we are not deceived or overwhelmed but tested, in accordance with what is said, "Test me, Lord, and try me" (Ps. 25:2). So with that harmful temptation which the Apostle means when he says, "Lest perhaps the tempter has tempted you, and our labour be in vain" (1 Thess. 3:5), God, as I said, tempts no one; that is, he brings or leads no one into temptation. For to be tempted and not to be brought into temptation is not bad; indeed it is even good, for this is to be tested. So when we say to God, "Do not bring us into temptation," what do we say but "Do not allow us to be brought in"? Hence some pray in this way, and it is read so in many manuscripts, and the most blessed Cyprian put it so: "Do not allow us to be led into temptation." In the Greek Gospel, however, I have nowhere found anything but "Do not bring us into temptation." We therefore live more safely if we give everything to God, and do not entrust ourselves partly to him and partly to ourselves; which this venerable martyr saw.
passages.notes: Several scanning errors corrected silently (e.g. 'Ii,. nas' read as 'sinas', 'amem' as 'autem'). Reference '(I Thess. III, £)' read as 3:5.

passages.original: Deus autem melius esse judicavit, miscere quosdam non perseveraturos certo numero sanctorum suorum; ut quibus non expedit in hujus vitæ tentatione securitas, non possint esse securi. Multos enim a perniciosa elatione reprimit quod ait Apostolus : Quapropter, qui videtur stare, videat ne cadat (( Cor. x, i£). Voluntate autem sua cadit, qui cadit; et voluntate Dei stat, qui stat. Potens est enim Deus statuere illum (Rom. XIV, 4): non ergo se ipse, sed Deus. Verumtamen bonum est non allum sapere, sed timere (Id. xi, 20). In cogitatione autem sua vel cadit quis.. que, vel stat. Sicut autem Apostolus alt, quod in libro superiore memoravi, Non sumus idonei cogitare aliquid quad ex nobismetipsis, aed sufficientia nostra ex Deo eat (II Cor. tu, 5). Quem seculus et beatas Ambrosius audet et dicit : Non enim in potestate nostra cor nostrum, et nostrœ cogitationes. Quod omnis qui humiliter et veraciter pius est, esse verissimum sentit.
passages.english: But God judged it better to mix some who will not persevere with the fixed number of his saints, so that those for whom security in the temptation of this life is not expedient may not be able to be secure. For what the Apostle says restrains many from destructive pride: "Therefore let him who seems to stand take heed lest he fall" (1 Cor. 10:12). But he who falls, falls by his own will; and he who stands, stands by the will of God. "For God is able to make him stand" (Rom. 14:4): not, then, he himself, but God. Nevertheless it is good not to be high-minded, but to fear (ibid. 11:20). And it is in his thought that each one either falls or stands. But as the Apostle says, as I mentioned in the preceding book, "We are not sufficient to think anything as of ourselves, but our sufficiency is from God" (2 Cor. 3:5). Following him, the blessed Ambrose too dares to say: "For our heart and our thoughts are not in our power." Which everyone who is humbly and truly devout feels to be most true.

passages.original: Cogitantes credimus, cogitantes loquimur, cogitantes agimus quidquid aginlus : quod autem attinet ad pictatis viam et verum Dei cultum, non samus idonei cogitare aliquid tanquam ex nobismetipsis, sed sufficientia nostra ex Deo est ( II Cor. III, 5 ). « Non enim est in potestate nostra cor nostram et nostrae cogitationes : » unde idem qui hoc ait, item dicit Ambrosius ( De Fuga sæculi, cap. 4), c Quis autem tam beatus qui in corde suo semper ascendat ? Sud hoc sine divino ausilio qui Heri potest ? nullo profecto modo. Denique, I Inquit, « supra eadem Scriptura dicit, Beatus vir cujus ut auxilium ejus abs te, Domine ; ascensus in corde ejus I ( Psal. LXXXIII, 6 ). Hoc utique ut diceret, non solum in Litteris sacris legebat, sed sicut de illo viro sine dubitatione credendum est, etiam in corde suo sentiebat Ambrosius.
passages.english: By thinking we believe, by thinking we speak, by thinking we do whatever we do; but as regards the way of piety and the true worship of God, "we are not sufficient to think anything as of ourselves, but our sufficiency is from God" (2 Cor. 3:5). "For our heart and our thoughts are not in our power"; hence the same Ambrose who says this also says (On Flight from the World, ch. 4): "But who is so blessed as always to ascend in his heart? But who can do this without divine help? In no way at all. Finally," he says, "the same Scripture says above, 'Blessed is the man whose help is from you, Lord; ascent is in his heart' (Ps. 83:6)." Ambrose, in order to say this, certainly not only read it in the sacred Letters, but, as must without doubt be believed of that man, also felt it in his heart.
passages.notes: Psalm numbered by the Vulgate (Ps. 84:5 in Hebrew numbering); 'cujus ut auxilium' read as 'cujus est auxilium'.

passages.original: ubi de initio fidei, quod etiam hoc donum Dei sit, quid sentiret ostendit: et pro perseverantia usque in finem, quia et ipsam nonnisi Deus eis qui perseveraverint donat, Ecclesiam Christi quotidie orare monstravit. Beatus quoque Ambrosius cum exponeret quod ait Lucas evan- gelisla, Visum eat et mihi (Luc. I, 3) : « Potest, I inquit, « non soli visum esse, quod sibi visum esse declarat. Non enim voluntate tantum humana visum est, sed sicut placuit ei qui in me loquitur Christus, qui ut id quod bonum est, nobis quoque videri bonum possit, operatur: quem enim miseratur, et vocat. Et ideo qui Christum sequitur, potest interrogatus cur esse vo.
passages.english: where he showed what he thought about the beginning of faith, that this too is a gift of God; and he showed that the Church of Christ prays daily for perseverance to the end, because God alone gives it to those who have persevered. The blessed Ambrose also, when expounding what the evangelist Luke says, "It seemed good to me also" (Luke 1:3), says: "What he declares seemed good to him can have seemed good not to him alone. For it did not seem good by human will alone, but as it pleased Christ who speaks in me, who works so that what is good may seem good to us also; for whom he has mercy on, he also calls.
